text:
Research supports distinguishing semantic alignment from popularity effects: [TASTE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports that text matching improves sequential recommendation while reducing popularity bias. This motivates—but does not establish—a matched permutation control: compare ID-only HSTU, HSTU with aligned text, and the same text-enabled architecture retrained with item texts shuffled within training-interaction popularity bins, additionally matching text length and missingness. Preserve missing-text masks and use a fixed item-to-text permutation consistently during training and inference. Aligned text outperforming shuffled text would support useful item–text alignment beyond these measured shortcuts; it would not prove causal semantic understanding. These are separate ablation trials, each producing one model per category; no prediction fusion or external pretrained weights are required.

Use identical validation users and the host’s fixed 99-negative candidate sets for paired per-user HR@10 differences; report category differences and their macro-average. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation, so conclusions must remain specific to the pinned sampled benchmark. Proposed uncertainty analysis: bootstrap paired user outcomes within each category, retaining equal category weights. Such intervals describe evaluation uncertainty conditional on the fitted models, not training variability.

Repeatedly choosing architectures, controls, or checkpoints using the same validation outcomes introduces adaptive selection bias; ordinary paired confidence intervals do not correct it. [Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629) establish the broader holdout-reuse problem. Predeclare a small ablation matrix, record every attempted configuration, and treat the selected validation improvement as exploratory pending the host’s separate held-out evaluation.
